title: Non-ketotic hyperglycaemia-induced hemichorea-hemiballism may represent glioma-like pattern on multimodal magnetic resonance imaging: can 1H spectroscopy help in the differentiation?
case_prompt: A 70-year-old man with a 20-year history of type 2 diabetes, poorly compliant with medications and glucose monitoring, presented with 2 days of severe involuntary movements of the right lower extremity. He had no ketonuria. Non-fasting plasma glucose was 9.08 mmol/L, serum osmolality 307.10 mOsm/L, and urinary ketones were negative. Noncontrast CT of the brain showed increased attenuation in the left putamen and caudate nucleus. MRI revealed heterogeneous hyperintensity in the same regions on T1-weighted images, an irregular hyperintense lesion with mild mass effect on T2-weighted and FLAIR sequences, and a ring-like enhancement on contrast-enhanced T1-weighted imaging. The lesion was iso- to hypo-intense on diffusion-weighted imaging. Single-voxel short-echo time 1H magnetic resonance spectroscopy demonstrated markedly increased lactate and lipid peaks, a slightly elevated choline peak, a slightly decreased N-acetylaspartate peak, and stable creatine, with a Cho/NAA ratio of 0.675, Cho/Cr of 1.04, NAA/Cr of 1.54, and (Lac + Lip)/Cr of 1.34.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Consideration of non-ketotic hyperglycaemia-induced hemichorea-hemiballism — “NKH-induced HC-HB is a rare reversible condition of poorly controlled type 2 diabetics.”  
2. Exclusion of high-grade glioma based on DWI — “DWI revealed no evidence of cytotoxic oedema or active cell proliferation (presented as restricted diffusion in patients with acute cerebral infarction or high-grade glioma) in the corresponding area.”  
3. Support for a metabolic/reversible process on MRS — “a relatively low Cho/NAA ratio (<1) suggested the diagnosis of a metabolic/reversible disease as revealed by our case.”  
4. Differentiation from other brain tumours (lymphoma, metastasis) — “brain tumours other than gliomas ... can exhibit a similarly pronounced increase in the Cho peak and a decrease in the NAA peak ... typically resulting in an inversion of the Hunter angle,” which was not seen here.  
5. Exclusion of central nervous system infection — “infectious diseases impacting the central nervous system seldom involve the unilateral basal ganglia in isolation. The MRI characteristics associated with these diseases demonstrate significant variability and are often non-specific...”
